daughter.prompt: a daughter of Eilhaud of Drassone, raised at court

draft.name: Dilhie Di Mesté
facts: She stands at five feet and six inches, with a slender frame that she maintains through daily riding and fencing practice in the castle yards.
Her eyes are large and amber-gold, with vertically slit pupils inherited from her Tsevranyan grandmother, though her skin is the warm olive tone of her Drassonais father's line.

Her hair is a deep chestnut brown, thick and slightly wavy, worn loosely braided or pinned up in court, though she favors simplicity over the elaborate arrangements fashionable among Drassonais ladies of her age.
Born in the autumn of 978, Ysolde is the only daughter and sole surviving child of Prince Eilhaud of Drassone and his first wife, the late Lady Thessaly of Vennemont.

She was raised at the Drassonais court from infancy, educated alongside noble children of the realm in languages, history, music, and deportment, with additional private instruction in Tsevrani by the same tutor her father once studied under.

Her mother, Lady Thessaly, died of a fever when Ysolde was seven years old, leaving her in the care of her father and the court household, a loss she has spoken of rarely but which shaped her into a quiet, self-reliant young woman.

She possesses her father's measured temperament but carries it with a warmth that puts even strangers at ease, a quality that has made her popular among the household staff and visiting dignitaries alike.

She has a sharp mind for politics, though she disguises her interest as idle curiosity rather than ambition, having learned early that overt intelligence in a woman at court invites unwanted attention.

She speaks Drassonais fluently with a refined accent and reads Tsevrani competently, though she speaks it with a halting, self-conscious cadence that betrays her as more comfortable in the written word than the spoken.
She is an accomplished rider and a passable fencer, trained in the Drassonais style by the castle master-at-arms, who privately admits she has more discipline than half the squires he teaches.
She is deeply devoted to her father, Eilhaud, and serves as a quiet confidante to him in matters of court life, offering observations about the mood of the nobility that his advisors sometimes miss.
She has no known suitors as of the year 1000, though rumors of matches with minor Drassonais lords and a Tsevranyan envoy's son have circulated in court gossip without confirmation.
marks: Thessaly is a historical region of Greece (ancient Thessalia).

owl_son.prompt: an owl-folk hunter who watches the stars, a son of Zakan

draft.name: Rostov Zakharyev Ul Yechra

person.name_meaning: from the east, son of Zakhary, of the Yechra clan
person.title: Huntsman

facts: Rostov stands slightly shorter than his father, with a lean, wiry build honed by decades of stalking prey through boreal forests and across frozen lake ice.
His plumage is a deep, rich white with sharp black barring across his wings and back — pristine and undiminished, unlike his father's aging coat.
His eyes are the characteristic pale yellow of Snowy Owl-folk, but brighter and sharper than Zakan's weathered gaze, with clean dark markings that frame them like a mask of ink on snow.
A faint scar traces the left side of his beak where it meets his face, a memento from a childhood tumble through a frozen creek bed that he tells differently depending on who's asking.
Born in 966 to Tsar Zakan III and a minor noblewoman of the Yechra clan named Yelena Ul Vostrikova, Rostov was the third of four sons, making him neither heir nor spare but something less certain.

He was raised in the hunting lodges of the northern provinces during his father's governorship, where he learned to track, trap, and read the behavior of every creature from lynx to lake trout before he could fly long distances.
Rostov possesses an unnatural patience while watching — he can remain motionless for hours on a tree branch or rocky outcrop, tracking the movement of stars as readily as the movement of prey below.
He is considered one of the finest long-range marksmen in Otsyenya, capable of bringing down a moose at three hundred paces with a bone-tipped arrow.
Unlike his methodical father, Rostov is quiet but restless, prone to long solitary walks along the shore of Vryushovsk that can last from dusk until dawn.
He speaks Varovni with a slower, softer cadence than Zakan, often trailing off into silence mid-sentence as though the words themselves have wandered off to watch the stars.
Zakan views his son with a mixture of quiet pride and gentle exasperation — he admires Rostov's skills but finds his tendency toward solitude difficult to reconcile with the duties of court life.
Rostov's three older brothers all died young — two of illness and one of a hunting accident in the taiga — leaving him, the youngest and least expected, as the sole surviving son of the Tsar.
